title: Meeting Rooms II
prompt: Given an array of meeting time intervals `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [start, end]`, return the minimum number of conference rooms required to hold all the meetings without any overlap within a room.

examples.explanation: One room hosts [0,30]; a second room hosts [5,10] then [15,20].
The meetings don't overlap, so one room suffices.
Meetings that only touch at an endpoint (one ends exactly when the next begins) don't count as overlapping, so a single room can handle all of them back-to-back.

hints: Think about the problem as tracking how many meetings are simultaneously in progress at any moment — the answer is the maximum of that count.
Separate all start times and all end times into two sorted lists, then sweep through them in time order.

Use two pointers over the sorted starts and sorted ends: whenever the next start is before the next end, a new room is needed (increment a counter); whenever a meeting ends, a room frees up (decrement). Track the running maximum.

solution.approach: Split the intervals into a sorted list of start times and a sorted list of end times. Sweep through both with two pointers: if the next start time is earlier than the next end time, a meeting is beginning before another ends, so we need an additional room (increment rooms and track the max); otherwise a room frees up (advance the end pointer). This simulates the number of concurrently active meetings without needing a heap.
solution.code:
def min_meeting_rooms(intervals):
    if not intervals:
        return 0

    starts = sorted(interval[0] for interval in intervals)
    ends = sorted(interval[1] for interval in intervals)

    s_ptr = 0
    e_ptr = 0
    rooms = 0
    max_rooms = 0

    while s_ptr < len(starts):
        if starts[s_ptr] < ends[e_ptr]:
            rooms += 1
            s_ptr += 1
            max_rooms = max(max_rooms, rooms)
        else:
            rooms -= 1
            e_ptr += 1

    return max_rooms
solution.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the sorted start/end arrays
